crisis without predictable funding streams who've seen their levels of

we see playing out highlights two distinct structural challenges that
Councillor Wolf's Motion directly addresses. A geographic divide and a
gender divide. First the geographic disparity. Cambridge remains a service

inventory, Kitchener Waterloo holds the vast majority of our region's

youth and supportive models like ship, the hart hub and
life launch. Meanwhile, Cambridge has a small fraction of that
capacity and what exists is restricted to narrow populations. For
an unhoused woman in Cambridge, there is zero transitional housing
in our city. When Transitional and Supportive Housing or other
pathways to permanent housing are scarce region - wide, emergency
shelters cannot function as intended. They become long - term
holding spaces for women with nowhere else to go. In
our Q1 data at YWCA Cambridge, out of 39 unique women
served, 11 were fully housing ready and sitting on region
wait list yet remain stuck in emergency beds. When half
of our 20 beds are frozen because there is nowhere
to transition. The door snaps shut for everyone else. And when
a warehousing unit finally opens up, it's almost always located
in Kitchener or Waterloo, forcing Cambridge women to abandon their
local support networks just to get a roof over their
heads. The only reason one of our senior residents finally
secured a home after 18 months and shelter was because
of one of our six dedicated patch rents supplements. Local
target investments work. We just need the region to plan
for them geographically. Furthermore, regional funding patterns consistently consolidate permanent
24 - 7 operating grants and kitchener waterloo by
leaving Cambridge providers scrambling to run part - time stopgaps,
like the afternoon - only drop - in at 150
Main or portraitslight seasonal warming centre. Temporary seasonal relief is
not a permanent solution for Cambridge. Second, the
the gender disparity. For unhoused women in Cambridge, our 20
emergency shelter beds are literally it. Because those beds are
constantly full. We have been unable to offer services for
over 270 requests we've received since August of 2025. And
we're unable to transitional exit ramps for these women. In
Kitchener facilities like ship on Frederick offer 39 dedicated transitional
beds for women and gender diverse individuals. In Cambridge, unless
a woman qualifies for sober living or is actively parenting
an infant. There is no transitional space for her. Her
only choice is to leave her community, her support network and
her city to move to Kitchener Waterloo if there is
space or remain on the street. When the system offers
co-ed spaces as an alternative, policy makers must confront the
reality. Co-ed spaces are not gender neutral. Research consistently shows
that women avoid Co-ed environments out of justified fears for
physical safety and exploitation. When a woman avoids a co
- ed space out of fear, that space is effectively
men only. Across the entire region there are only
42 dedicated emergency women's shelter beds 20 in Cambridge, 22
in Kitchener. Meanwhile, 80 beds and Cambridge are dedicated to
men in the remainder of the 400 to 500 regional
shelter beds are men only or co-ed. Women are simply being left
out of the system design. The region of Waterloo holds
a sole jurisdictional mandate of service manager to allocate Homelessness
funds fairly across all municipalities. Equitable distribution does not mean
taking resources away from our neighbours. Rather it means using
governance tools to prevent those divides from widening. This motion
introduces three vital mechanisms, evaluating major capital investments over 1

build permanent shelter and supportive housing capacity in Cambridge. And
firmly applying a gender - based analysis plus lens across
all Homelessness funding so women are no longer deprioritized. We
cannot solve a regional crisis with a centralized infrastructure strategy.
